Learning Objectives
Understand the basic pathoanatomy of congenital dislocation of the knee.
Discuss nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for congenital dislocation of the knee.
Recognize the conditions commonly associated with congenital dislocation of the knee and
understand how to approach management of concurrent hip and foot conditions.
Understand the basic pathoanatomy of congenital dislocation of the patella.
Review the basic history and physical examination for congenital dislocation of the patella and
explain the reason diagnosis often is delayed.
Discuss treatment approaches for congenital dislocation of the patella.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Congenital dislocation of the knee is a rare disorder that occurs sporadically and occasionally
within families.
Associated with conditions that produce muscle imbalance or laxity (eg, myelodysplasia,
arthrogryposis, Larsen syndrome)
Epidemiology
The estimated incidence of congenital dislocation of the knee is 1 per 100,000 live births.
Associated with breech positioning
Associated with laxity disorders, such as Larsen syndrome, and neuromuscular conditions,
such as myelodysplasia and arthrogryposis
Approximately 40% to 100% of patients with congenital dislocation of the knee have additional
musculoskeletal issues.
Developmental dysplasia of the hip and clubfoot are commonly associated with congenital
dislocation of the knee.
Multiple nonmusculoskeletal issues as well

Epidemiology
A 1985 Scandinavian study estimated a regional rate of 17 cases of congenital dislocation
of the knee per 1 million individuals or 1% of the rate of developmental dislocation of the
hip.1 Regarding associated conditions, a collection of 155 cases of congenital dislocation
of the knee from multiple hospitals revealed a 45% rate of concurrent hip dysplasia, a
31% rate of concurrent congenital foot deformities (mostly clubfoot), and a 10% rate of
concurrent congenital elbow dislocations.2 The association between congenital
dislocation of the knee and breech positioning is unclear; the knee being forced into
hyperextension by breech positioning and knee extension blocking normal spontaneous
cephalic version have been suggested.3

Anatomy and Biomechanics
In congenital dislocation of the knee, the tibia is anteriorly dislocated, with the femoral
condyles displaced posteriorly in the popliteal space.
Fundamental pathologic features4
Shortening of the quadriceps tendon
Tight anterior capsule
Hypoplasia of the suprapatellar bursa
Osteology
With congenital dislocation of the knee, the patella is adherent to the anterior aspect of the
distal femur,5 may be displaced laterally,6 or may be absent.7
Epiphyseal deformity is more notable in older children.8
Anterior bowing of the tibia may occur.7,8
Hypoplasia of the femur and tibia; absence of the proximal fibula7
Tendons
The quadriceps tendon is adherent to the anterior aspect of the femur4-6,9 and has
fibrosis.5,6,10
Medial hamstrings are positioned anterior to the flexion axis of the knee and function as
extensors.6,9,11
Iliotibial band insertion also may be displaced,7 and the fascia lata may be contracted and
adherent to the vastus lateralis, contributing to a lateral rotation deformity.5
Joints and Ligaments
The suprapatellar pouch is hypoplastic or obliterated and replaced by fibrofatty tissue.1,4,6,9,11
The medial and lateral collateral ligaments are displaced over the femoral condyles.9
More than one-third of patients may have lateral rotation deformity of the tibia.5
Some studies have noted a lack of cruciate ligaments,2 whereas other studies have reported
that they are present but stretched out.1
Musculature

The gastrocnemius heads may displace laterally.8
The vastus lateralis inserts more proximally than normal.1
Etiology
Multiple potential causes of congenital dislocation of the knee have been proposed.
Genetic origin; however, only a small percentage of patients have a family history
Intrauterine restriction
Neuromuscular imbalance
Cases associated with syndromes generally are more severe.
Mild cases may be primarily the result of intrauterine positioning.

Etiology
The etiology of congenital dislocation of the knee remains unknown. Studies have
reported on patients with a family history of the condition; however, in a study of 200
dislocations, a family history was confirmed in only seven patients.12 Genetic causes are
suspected because of the association between knee dislocations and hip dysplasia,
clubfoot, and congenital vertical talus, which also have a genetic origin.6 Intrauterine
factors also may play a role. A study reported premature rupture of the membranes,
oligohydramnios, and/or dysfunctional labor in all 17 cases of congenital knee
dislocations.13 Neuromuscular imbalance,1,14 and absence or hypoplasia of the cruciate
ligaments also have been proposed as causes;2 however, some studies have
hypothesized that cruciate pathology is more likely secondary to the dislocations.1 In
patients with more mild congenital dislocation of the knee, which may resolve without
management, congenital postural deformity (eg, conditions such as calcaneovalgus foot)
may be the cause.15 In general, syndromic congenital knee dislocations tend to be more
severe than idiopathic congenital knee dislocations,4 and bilateral dislocations suggest a
syndromic or neuromuscular etiology.
Natural History

Younger children with a congenital knee dislocation are able to walk if untreated but only with
the knee in flexion.
Without treatment, persistent hyperextension and lack of full knee flexion are present.

Natural History
A report on three juvenile children with congenital dislocation of five knees found that all
the patients walked with the knees dislocated and in mild flexion of 15° to 20°, with
flexion limited to 90° and hyperextension of at least 20° but with painless range of
motion.2 Given the known mechanical issues with walking in knee flexion, activity is
expected to be notably limited if the condition remains unmanaged into adulthood.
Classification
The most common classification system for congenital knee dislocations is based on knee
position (Figure 1).
Grade I: severe knee recurvatum, joint reduced
Grade II: anterior subluxation of the tibia
Grade III: anterior dislocation of the tibia
An alternative classification system, which excludes patients with only recurvatum, has been
associated with ultimate knee flexion range of motion after management.16
Type I: easily reducible and stable in flexion (Figure 2)
Type II: reducible but dislocates if reduction force is removed (Figure 3)
Type III: irreducible (Figure 4)
Most studies using the common classification system exclude patients who have severe knee
recurvatum but no joint subluxation or dislocation.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
In infants with congenital dislocation of the knee, the knee may be hyperextended, and the
foot is easily placed against the face. Knee flexion is limited.
A dimple or skin crease is observed at the anterior knee.
Hip and foot examinations are important given associated conditions at both sites.
Patient History
Congenital dislocation of the knee generally is noted at birth; however, it also may be
diagnosed during the prenatal period.
Physical Examination
Anterior dislocation of the tibia with respect to the femur
Recurvatum deformity of the knee
The posterior aspect of the femoral condyles is palpable in the popliteal fossa.
Assessment of joint reduction may help determine prognosis.
Valgus deformity may occur.
Anterior skin grooves
More skin grooves suggest a better prognosis16 (Figure 2).
A lack of skin grooves indicates a poor prognosis and suggests arthrogryposis (Figure 4).

Physical Examination
Hyperextension of the knee is universally present in patients with congenital dislocation
of the joint. Reducibility of the knee and more anterior skin grooves indicate a better
prognosis.
Imaging Studies

Lateral radiographs most commonly are used to diagnose congenital dislocation of the knee
and to monitor management.
Radiography
A lateral radiograph differentiates simple hyperextension from subluxation or dislocation
(Figure 1).
An arthrogram may demonstrate lack of a suprapatellar pouch.4,17
Delayed ossification of the distal femur17

Radiography
One study reported on a child with a congenital knee dislocation who had 90° of knee
flexion but persistent dislocation, emphasizing the importance of lateral radiography to
monitor management.18
Ultrasonography
Prenatal ultrasonography may be used to diagnose congenital knee dislocation.19
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be used to assess the cruciate ligaments.
Management
Management of a knee dislocation takes priority over management of ipsilateral hip dysplasia
or clubfoot. For example, knee flexion is required with the use of a Pavlik harness for hip
management and clubfoot casts.
Nonsurgical Management
Management of congenital knee dislocation begins with stretching, followed by serial cast or
splint immobilization (Figure 5).

Flexion should be attempted after the tibia has been reduced on the end of the femur (ie,
reduction can be confirmed via a lateral radiograph or ultrasonography). Distal femoral
physeal separation or plastic deformity of the tibia is possible.
Prognosis generally is excellent if reduction is achieved nonsurgically.
Figure 5 Images of an infant with a congenital knee dislocation shows management with the use
of an anterior splint. (Reproduced with permission from Rampal V, Mehrafshan M,
Ramanoudjame M, Seringe R, Glorion C, Wicart P: Congenital dislocation of the knee at birth: Part
2. Impact of a new classification on treatment strategies, results and prognostic factors. Orthop
Traumatol Surg Res 2016;102[5]:635-638.)

Nonsurgical Management
For serial cast or splint immobilization of a dislocated knee, an anterior-based force must
be placed on the distal femur and a posterior-based force must be placed on the
proximal tibia to stretch the quadriceps and reduce the joint. Some studies recommend
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:45 AM
AAOS | Congenital Dislocation of the Knee and Patella
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000524
12/27

traction if serial cast immobilization is not successful.5,20 A Pavlik harness also may be
used; a study reported success even in patients who had disappointing results with
splinting.21 With a Pavlik harness, hip flexion relaxes the rectus and the tensor fascia lata
and, assuming the hips are reduced, helps tension the hamstrings so they function as
knee flexors.21 Most clinicians consider management successful if the femoral tibial joint
has been reduced and 90° of knee flexion has been attained, with surgical management
scheduled if these parameters cannot be achieved.6
In general, the hip and foot are managed after the knee has been reduced and adequate
flexion has been attained. In terms of the hip, knee flexion is necessary to prevent
hamstring tension from pulling the femoral head superior and lateral.14 In terms of the
foot, the gastrocnemius remains under tension until the knee is flexed.14 Those who
manage the knee and foot concurrently concede that foot correction is easier after 90°
of knee flexion is attained.22
Surgical Management
Surgical management of congenital dislocation of the knee should always include quadriceps
lengthening.
Best outcomes are observed if surgical treatment is performed in children younger than 6
months.
Indications
Surgical management is indicated if nonsurgical management fails to reduce the tibia on the
end of the femur or if the knee cannot be flexed to 90°.
Patients with neuromuscular disease are more likely to require surgical treatment than those
without neuromuscular disease.
A study suggested that surgery should be the primary treatment option for congenital knee
dislocation if the joint is not reducible on presentation.20
Techniques/Procedures
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Congenital Dislocation of the Knee and Patella


Techniques/Procedures
Although quadriceps lengthening always is included in the surgical management of
congenital knee dislocations, transverse release of the capsule often is required to
achieve adequate knee flexion.4,8,22 The tensor fascia lata and the vastus lateralis also
may need to be released.5 In addition, some surgeons have advocated for advancement
of the anterior cruciate ligament,8 and other surgeons have advocated for physeal-
sparing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.23 To allow for reduced quadriceps
lengthening, femoral shortening has been advocated, particularly in patients with hip
and knee dislocations.24
Complications
Fracture
Deformities of the femur and tibia and frank fractures have been reported with
splinting.15,18,20 A study found that 10 of 19 dislocated knees had a fracture or injury close to
the physis.1
Instability
Recurrent subluxation requiring revision surgery has been reported.6 This may occur
secondary to insufficient quadriceps lengthening.25
Other Complications
Wound healing issues may occur with the large incision required for quadricepsplasty.25
Outcomes
Idiopathic dislocations tend to result in better outcomes.4,6
Extensor lag is commonly observed but does not appear to result in major functional
problems.22

14/27

Persistent instability is common, with a study reporting a positive pivot shift in one-half of
patients at follow-up.7

Outcomes
A study on how the original classification system of congenitally dislocated knees
affected treatment selection and prognosis reported that four of seven congenitally
dislocated knees that could be maintained in a reduced position on initial evaluation had
good or excellent outcomes. Conversely, all the knees that were irreducible on initial
evaluation had poor outcomes.20 Another study comparing the results of dislocated hips
and knees managed concurrently versus those managed in a staged fashion (ie, with the
hip managed after the knee was able to flex sufficiently) reported comparable results;24
however, the knees managed concurrent with the hips appeared to have better range of
motion, stability, and extensor function, favoring simultaneous management in knees
managed surgically.24
Instability also is common with congenital dislocation of the knee. Although some
studies have noted that children do well without any bracing,26 other studies have
reported poor results5 or the need for subsequent joint stabilizing procedures, such as
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction or posterior capsulorrhaphy, in patients with
instability.24 Early surgical management generally is thought to result in better
outcomes, with one study reporting better results in children treated immediately on
diagnosis versus at 3 to 4 months of age11,14 and another study showing that the upper
age limit for a satisfactory outcome with initial treatment was 2 years.13
Congenital Dislocation of the Patella
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Congenital dislocation of the patella is a rare disorder.
Because of the delayed ossification and small size of the patella, diagnosis often is delayed.

Overview
Congenital dislocation of the patella is a rare condition in which the patella is irreducible at
birth.
Congenital dislocation of the patella should be suspected in a young child with a knee flexion
contracture unless an explanation, such as arthrogryposis or obvious congenital deformity,
exists.
Epidemiology
Associated with foot deformities, such as clubfoot, calcaneal valgus, and congenital vertical
talus
Also associated with developmental delays and other anomalies

Epidemiology
Congenital dislocation of the patella is a very rare disorder, with limited small case series
and reports in the literature. A study of 12 patients with the disorder found that 11 had
another anomaly, general dysplasia, or developmental delay.27
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The patella is dislocated and fixed over the lateral distal femur via soft-tissue contractures and
occasionally pseudoarticulation with the distal femur.
The tibial tubercle insertion is laterally positioned on the proximal tibia.
The knee joint is in valgus and external rotation.

Anatomy and Biomechanics

The pathoanatomy of congenital dislocation of the patella is based on intraoperative
findings during correction27-29 and on the analysis of a stillborn fetus.30 The primary
problem is thought to be external rotation of the entire extensor mechanism.31
Osteology
The patella, which is hypoplastic with a flattened articular surface, is fixed on the lateral aspect
of the lateral femoral condyle.
The trochlea is shallow and contains fatty tissue.
The anterior aspect of the lateral femoral condyle also is flattened.
Severe external torsion of the proximal tibia and internal torsion of the remainder of the tibia
are present, with the ankle mortise in line with the distal femur.
The tibial tubercle is substantially lateral, in line with the outer aspect of the lateral femoral
condyle.
The fibular head is displaced posteriorly.
Genu valgum is a common deformity.
Tendons
The quadriceps is contracted.
The patellar tendon is malrotated and inserts on the anterolateral proximal tibia so the
quadriceps may become a flexor of the knee.
The iliotibial band is contracted, inserts deep to the patella, and is adherent to the posterior
border of the patella.
The biceps tendon is contracted.
The pes anserinus generally is normal, adding flexion to the knee.
The gastrocnemius generally is normal.
Joints and Ligaments
A pseudoarticulation may occur between the patella and the lateral femoral condyle.
External rotatory and/or lateral femorotibial subluxation may occur.
The lateral capsule is contracted.
The medial retinaculum is thin and elongated and may adhere to the intercondylar notch and
the lateral femoral condyle.

Musculature
The proximal aspects of the rectus femoris and the vastus lateralis are laterally positioned, and
the vastus intermedialis may be absent.
Etiology
In patients with congenital dislocation of the patella, a myotome containing the quadriceps
muscle is thought to improperly rotate internally during development.31
Natural History
Many patients with congenital dislocation of the patella are pain free and asymptomatic.
However, in a study of congenital and obligatory patellar dislocations, all the patients 7 years
and older had pain and functional limitations secondary to lack of knee extension power and
full extension.32
Valgus deformity and tibial subluxation are thought to increase during development.27
Classification

Classification
Although no classification system for congenital patellar dislocation is widely used, some
surgeons insist that only patients born with an irreducible patella have the disorder.
Other surgeons consider patients in whom an irreducible patellar dislocation develops
during childhood as having the diagnosis, including patients with underlying Down
syndrome, nail-patellar syndrome, Kabuki syndrome, or Ellis-Van Creveld syndrome.29
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Although early management of congenital patellar dislocation is beneficial in avoiding
secondary deformity, diagnosis often is delayed because the patella is small and has delayed
ossification.
In any child with an unexplainable knee flexion contracture, a small patella laterally over the
lateral femoral condyle should be suspected.

If a child has a knee flexion contracture without arthrogryposis or other congenital
abnormality, congenital patellar dislocation should be considered.31
Patient History
Knee flexion contracture
Some children have delayed ambulation.
An associated foot deformity is very common.
Physical Examination
In a study on congenital patellar dislocation, the mean knee flexion contracture was 28o
(range, 5o to 60o).29
Lack of full active knee extension
At 90o of flexion, the quadriceps, with its abnormal insertion, cannot extend the knee and acts
as a flexor.28
Genu valgum
External rotation deformity of the knee

Physical Examination
In some children with congenital dislocation of the patella, gait may appear essentially
normal; therefore, assessment for knee flexion contracture, active knee extension lag,
and ability to palpate the patella on the lateral aspect of the knee are important.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The patella typically ossifies at age 3 to 5 years; however, this may be delayed in children with
congenital dislocation of the patella.
In older children, a sunrise radiograph reliably demonstrates the patella; in younger children,
the patella may be difficult to visualize on AP and lateral views.

Ultrasonography/MRI
Ultrasonography or MRI can be used to confirm patellar dislocation in a younger child with an
unossified patella (Figure 6); however, neither is necessary if the diagnosis is certain.
An advantage of ultrasonography is the lack of sedation.
MRI is beneficial for evaluating the shallowness of the trochlea, the tibial tubercle position, and
other anatomic issues.
Figure 6 MRI of the knee of a 3-year-old girl with a congenital knee dislocation shows a laterally
displaced, hypoplastic patella with severe trochlear dysplasia/an absent trochlea. (Reproduced
from McIntosh AL: Congenital dislocation of the knee and congenital patellar dislocations, in

Martus JE, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Pediatrics, ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2022, pp 317-320.)
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of congenital patellar dislocation is based on a fixed lateral dislocation of the patella.
Differential Diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis
A study reported on two patients with previously unrecognized patellar dislocation who
were treated via femoral osteotomy for genu valgum;27 this emphasizes the importance
of a high index of suspicion for congenital dislocation of the patella, particularly in
younger children. The disorder also must be differentiated from common obligatory
subluxation, which occurs in juvenile to adolescent patients.
Management
Surgical management is requisite for congenital patellar dislocation and involves extensive
mobilization of the extensor mechanism, with release of lateral restraints and medialization of
the patellar tendon insertion.
Nonsurgical Management
Serial cast or brace immobilization may be used preoperatively to improve the knee flexion
contracture.28,29
The patella cannot be reduced via nonsurgical methods.
Surgical Management
In younger children, congenital dislocation of the patella generally is managed to avoid
potential pain and future functional issues and to avoid secondary genu valgum and external
rotation deformity of the knee.

In adolescents or adults without pain or functional issues, patellar dislocations may be
managed nonsurgically.
Techniques/Procedures
Three main approaches have been described for the management of congenital dislocation of
the patella.33
In immature patients, proximal release of the quadriceps, advancement of the vastus
medialis obliquus, and medial transfer of the patellar tendon; in mature patients, tibial
tubercle osteotomy32
Lateral release and partial transfer of the patellar insertion
Extensive distal lateral release, transfer of the patella into a new synovial pocket, and medial
transfer of the patellar tendon27 (Figure 7)
Figure 7 Illustrations of a knee show surgical management of a congenital dislocation of the
patella. A, Lateral view shows an S-shaped skin incision, which is made beginning approximately
5 cm above the lateral femoral condyle, over the dislocated patella, extending to the medial side
distal to the proximal growth plate of the tibia and to the medial side of the tibial diaphysis. B,
Coronal view shows detachment of the skin with the fat layer from the patellar retinaculum and
the adjacent structures via blunt preparation. C, Lateral view shows exposure and oblique
division of the tight iliotibial band and the biceps femoris tendon. D, Coronal view shows
detachment of the patellar tendon from its insertion with no cartilage. The tendon is freed from
the retinaculum. The medial retinaculum is split transversely. The proximal parts of the
retinaculum and the distal parts of the vasti are detached from the synovial membrane via blunt
preparation. The membrane is excised from the edges of the patella, and the resulting opening in
the synovial cavity is closed with the use of suture. The patella and its tendon with a buried
strong suture are passed through an opening made in the synovial membrane. The tendon is

passed out through an opening made in the capsule. The patella remains in the closed synovial
cavity. The tendon is buried in a hole in the metaphysis. (Reproduced with permission from

Postoperative Management
Protocols vary but generally involve 2 to 6 weeks of immobilization followed by gradual range
of motion of the knee.
Weight bearing may be relatively quick with the knee in extension.
Physiotherapy is important for regaining range of motion.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
A more standard lateral release and medial imbrication or reconstruction, which may be
attempted for recurrent patellar dislocation, is inadequate to address the level of pathology
with congenital dislocation of the patella.
Complications
In congenital dislocation of the patella, neuropraxia may occur with acute correction of a large
knee flexion contracture.
Recurrent dislocation has been reported in multiple studies because of the complex pathology
of congenital dislocation of the patella, including the shallow trochlea;5,34 however, studies
emphasize balancing alignment intraoperatively.1-3,5-7
Caution to avoid overtightening, which may result in medial dislocation
The risk of wound infection is higher given the large incisions generally used.

Complications
A study on 11 children (17 knees) with congenital dislocation of the patella reported one
case of peroneal nerve neuropraxia, one redislocation of the patella, and one superficial
wound infection.32

Outcomes
After surgical management of 17 knees with congenital dislocation of the patella, a study
reported that extension lag improved from 15° to 2°.32
The same study noted that seven of eight patients with bilateral disease opted to undergo
treatment for the opposite knee after surgical management of the more pathologic side.32
Most case series have noted improvement in patients after treatment, with maintained
reduction in most patients and improved knee extension function.
